keyVerseText: And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;
rootMeaning: The root of פַּשְׁחוּר (Pashchûwr) likely comes from the Hebrew root פָּשַׁח (pâshach), which means to tear or pull in pieces. This etymological background suggests a notion of liberation or breaking free, as tearing apart can imply releasing or setting free. Thus, beyond a mere proper name, the root sense conveys an idea of freedom or deliverance, adding depth to the name Pashur as one associated with release or emancipation.
usageInScripture: The word פַּשְׁחוּר appears 14 times in the Hebrew Scriptures, predominantly as a proper name for several Israelite individuals, including priests and temple officials. It is mostly translated simply as "Pashur" or "of Pashur," highlighting its use as a personal name rather than a common noun. The consistency in translation across occurrences emphasizes its identity function rather than a conceptual term, yet the underlying meaning of freedom remains implicit in the name's origin.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פַּשְׁחוּר as rooted in the concept of liberation enriches our appreciation of biblical names and their theological resonance. Names in Scripture often convey God's purposes or attributes, and Pashur's connection to freedom can remind believers of God's power to liberate His people. Even as some bearers of the name were involved in challenging moments of Israel's history, the name itself points to the hope of deliverance that God provides. This reflects the broader biblical theme of God breaking the bonds of sin and captivity through Christ, the ultimate source of true freedom.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 9:12, the name Pashur appears as an ancestor of Adaiah, situating him within a priestly lineage connected to temple service. The verse reads, "And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah..." Here, Pashur's name not only identifies a historical figure but also subtly evokes the heritage of liberation and service to God. This lineage underscores the faithfulness and continuity of God's people, who serve Him across generations, embodying the freedom and covenant relationship implied in the name Pashur.
